title: Field Operator Gazette — On‑Prem Control Plane: Setup, Scale Waves & Rotation Guide
body:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic, field‑operator focused runbook for commissioning, scaling, and rotating Redwood’s private control plane in vpc/on‑prem environments. It collects the experiments, gotchas, and minimal safe steps we use in lab and on customer sites. Intended audience: oncall operator, SREs doing field installs, and solutions engineers running first installs for customers.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target: private control plane (k8s + controlplane services + controlplane DB + S3/compatible object store + KMS integration).
- Network: customer VPC or isolated onprem network with NAT and private DNS available.
- Prescribed Terraform modules from infra repo; we assume remote state with locking (consul/terraform cloud/S3+dynamo).
- This is not the full security binder — assume customer infra team owns firewall/VPC peering steps.

TL;DR checklist (quick skim):
1) Verify preflight: DNS records, KMS access, object store bucket, NTP sync on nodes, time skew < 300ms.
2) Ensure remote state lock works (test with a dry-run apply in a sandbox).
3) Bootstrap minimal control plane (API server + etcd/postgres operator + ingress).
4) Run smoke: health-check, token issuance, small inference job against local model runner.
5) Scale waves in 3 increments, validating KV cache warm and request fan‑out.
6) Rotation: drain node -> disable ingress -> upgrade controlplane -> rejoin node -> verify.

Prereqs (detailed):
- Terraform CLI version pinned (see module notes below).
- kubectl and kubeconfig for admin context.
- Access to customer KMS with key ARN and decrypt/encrypt test permission.
- Sufficient ephemeral capacity for canary wave (usually +1 small GPU node).

Terraform module notes (practical hints):
- Pin provider versions in root module: aws ~> 5.0 OR k8s provider >= 2.25.
- Use feature-flag variable map: var.feature_flags = { enable_telemetry = true, enable_rolling_windows = true } to avoid surprising defaults when modules change.
- When changing module inputs that alter computed resource names, add a migration plan: create new resource with new name, switch traffic, then destroy old. Don’t rely on Terraform rename unless it’s exact resource id change.
- State locking: always validate lock-provider prior to large changes. We once lost a plan because S3 backend had eventual consistency; set max_retries for state locking.
- Module composition: break modules into network, infra-base, k8s-bootstrap, cp-services. During upgrades, you can apply infra-base and k8s-bootstrap separately to reduce blast radius.
- Partial applies: allowed for non-shared resources (e.g., node pools) but avoid partial apply for core DB schemas. If you must, take manual DB snapshot first.
- Secrets handling: Terraform should write sealed secrets to object storage; never store raw KMS keys in tfstate. Use remote secret backend (vault) for ephemeral creds.

Initial bootstrap sequence (stepwise):
1) Preflight document signoff (Slack thread + checklist): owner, maintenance window, rollback owner.
2) DNS and LB targets: create CNAMEs internal to VPC; verify discovery across AZs.
3) Apply network → infra-base modules (up to k8s bootstrap). Validate: nodes join, kube-system pods ready.
4) Apply k8s-bootstrap: RBAC, cert-manager, metrics-server. Wait for cert-manager to issue CP certs.
5) Apply cp-services with replicas set to 1 for critical control plane services.
6) DB bring-up: prefer managed Postgres where possible. If using self-hosted, create PVCs with replication and run initial schema migrations in maintenance mode.
7) Smoke: create test tenant, request token, call /health and /v1/generate against local small model.

Scale wave pattern (recommended):
- Wave 0 (canary): Add +1 worker, increase critical cp service replicas to 2 where safe, validate GC, KV cache hit stabilization for 15m.
- Wave 1 (core scale): Increase pod replicas to target minimum (usually 50% of expected steady state), add node pool if needed. Run synthetic traffic matching P50 latency budget.
- Wave 2 (full): Reach steady capacity. Run load testing for 1–2 hours, watch for queue building upstream and OOMs.

Key observations from lab runs:
- KV cache warm is a latency multiplier: initial requests have 3–8x token cost until cache warms (plan for warmup traffic).
- Autoscaler hysteresis can cause churn when bursty traffic collides with batching windows; tune scaleDownDelay to avoid thrash.
- Network MTU mismatches on onprem switches lead to gRPC fragmentation errors; default to 1400 MTU for tunnels.

Rotation protocol (node/service rotation without downtime):
1) Pre-rotation: mark node as maintenance in inventory, disable new scheduling at LB / route.
2) Drain: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node>. Watch for controlplane pods that cannot be moved — those must be manually moved with replicated replicas.
3) Service pause: for storage or DB schema upgrades consider readonly mode (reconfigure traffic router to read-only tenants).
4) Upgrade binary/image on node and run health probes locally (curl localhost:8080/healthz, etc.).
5) Rejoin node: remove maintenance flag, enable routing. Monitor request heatmap and tail error rates for 30 minutes.

Upgrade plan (control plane version bump):
- Strategy: staggered canary deploy + canary route testing + automated rollback. Don’t mix control plane and DB schema changes in same release.
- Canary cohort: 5% traffic by route tagging (route policy) or separate ingress group. Run fuzzed inference for signoff (automated eval harness).
- DB migrations: run offline migrations as background tasks that are backward compatible. If migration is destructive, create migration with lock-step switch: deploy migration agent -> mark read-only -> apply -> verify -> mark read‑write.
- KMS rotation: perform rewrap in small batches (10 keys at a time) and watch for KMS throttling. Plan for increased retries.

Rollback play (fastest safe path):
- If canary fails: immediately reroute canary traffic back to previous controlplane (route swap) and trigger rollback pipeline that redeploys previous image.
- If full cluster shows systemic failure: scale down new pods to 0 for the service, restore DB from pre-upgrade snapshot if corruption suspected.
- Stateful mismatch: take immediate snapshots of DB and object store, maintain immutable copies for postmortem.

Observability & verification checklist post-change:
- API error rate (5xx) at cluster and per-route level should be <= baseline + 0.5%.
- Tail latency p99 should not increase by more than configured SLO delta (default 10%).
- KV cache hitrate recovers to pre-change baseline within 30–60 minutes.
- Cost estimation: token-per-second and GPU utilization; ensure batching efficacy hasn’t regressed.
- E2E customer tests: for first 10 customers, run synthetic requests and token accounting checks.

Troubleshooting quick hits (common failure modes):
- Postgres connection storms: check connection pool config and max_connections; scale pooler or increase connection limits.
- Ingress hotswap flapping: verify LB healthcheck intervals and DNS TTLs.
- KMS denied operations: confirm IAM principal used by controlplane has kms:Decrypt and kms:Encrypt on the key; test via aws kms decrypt on a test blob.
- Unexpected OOMs after upgrade: check new binary memory profile, revert image, open issue for memory regression.

Operational notes & heuristics (from operator lab):
- Always run schema migrations twice in staging with production-like data size; timebudget is often 10x longer in prod because of indexes.
- Prefer add‑back scaling (adding instances) during daytime windows and subtracting during low traffic windows.
- Use feature gates to switch new behavior off immediately without a redeploy when possible.

Appendix A: useful commands (operator cheat sheet)
- Terraform plan: terraform init && terraform plan -out=plan.out && terraform show -json plan.out | jq .
- Test state lock: terraform state pull (ensure not raising lock errors)
- Drain a node: kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m
- Check CP pod health: kubectl get pods -n redwood-cp -o wide | grep -E "CrashLoop|Error"
- Snapshot DB (Postgres): pg_dump -Fc -f pre-upgrade-YYYYMMDD.dump || use cloud snapshot api if managed.

Open questions / TODOs (operational):
- Decide default KV cache warmup traffic template and add to onboarding script.
- Add automated canary traffic generator that mimics target tenant mix (P50/P90).
- Formalize exact state snapshot gating rules for Terraform partial applies.

Field notes (operator voice):
- "We hit two surprises on site A: the customer’s firewall rewrote internal DNS so cert-manager failed to validate. Added step: validate resolver for cert-manager in preflight." — Marcus Li
- "On wave 1 we saw a persistent 502 against the worker pool; turned out to be MTU mismatch on the VPN side — switching to 1400 fixed it." — Priya Nair

End of gazette. Keep this doc as the living field notes for teams running first installs; update after each field rotation with date-tagged notes.
